correctness.rationale: For every \(q=2^n\ge4\), the affine function \(X^{q+2}+X\) is not a square (its derivative is \(1\)), ensuring integrality. The partial derivatives \(F_X=Z^{q+1}\) and \(F_Z=XZ^q\) force the unique singularity \(P\) and tangent \(Z=0\). Comparison of \(F(M)=\rho F\) for a point-and-tangent-preserving matrix yields \(b=c=g=0\), \(\lambda^{q+1}=1\), and \(f/a=\lambda^2\), with converse by direct substitution. The first-order constraint has rank five in the nine matrix variables, giving Lie dimension three after scalar quotient. Matrices with \(a^q=b^q=0\) and \(c^q=1\) preserve \(F\) over every base algebra and give the subgroup scheme \((\alpha_q)^2\rtimes\mu_q\) of length \(q^3\). Finitely many geometric points imply the stabilizer is finite, and group translation gives length at least \((q+1)q^3\). Exact arithmetic independently verifies \(\mathbb F_4\) point counts and first-order ranks for \(q\in\{4,8,16\}\). The reduced diagonal subgroup \(\mu_{q+1}\) normalizes the connected subgroup by weights \(\lambda^2\) and \(\lambda\). Their intersection is trivial; the finite closed semidirect product \(K_q\) therefore has exact length \(q^3(q+1)\) and contains all geometric-point symmetries and Lie directions.

value.rationale: The final narrow statement constructs a finite subgroup scheme K_q of exact length q^3(q+1), with a connected factor of height n and length q^3, integrating all three previously known infinitesimal directions and the complete reduced point group. Knowledge of an abstract Lie algebra or geometric group does not guarantee such a simultaneous higher-order group-scheme action. As q increases this gives a uniform, unbounded measure of the nonreduced projective stabilizer. It is a motivated structural strengthening of existing data rather than a routine new parameter choice; exact full stabilizer length is left open.
